title: Two paths: shortening once, redirecting forever
description: A URL is shortened once and resolved millions of times. The write path can afford coordination; the read path cannot, so it is served almost entirely from cache.

steps.text: A client submits a long URL. This happens once per link, so a little latency here is affordable.

The API gets a unique short key. Base-62 encoding a counter guarantees uniqueness with no collision check; hashing the URL instead means handling collisions. Seven characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion keys.
The mapping is written to the store, sharded by key so writes spread evenly. The short URL is returned.
A browser requests the short URL. This path runs at perhaps 10× the write rate and must be fast.
The API checks the cache. Links follow a steep popularity curve, so a small cache absorbs the large majority of reads.
On a miss it reads the store and populates the cache. Because mappings are immutable once created, entries never need invalidating — which makes this one of the easiest caches to operate.

It responds with a redirect. 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache it and skips your servers entirely next time; 302 (temporary) keeps every click coming to you so you can count it. That is an analytics-versus-load decision, not a technical one.
